# Book I, Proposition 5

*The base angles of an isosceles triangle*

> In isosceles triangles the angles at the base are equal to one another, and, if the equal straight lines be produced further, the angles under the base will be equal to one another.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/05-idea.svg" alt="Make two sides equal (blue), and the angles at the base are equal (yellow), and so are the angles under it (red)." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Make two sides equal (blue), and the angles at the base are equal (yellow), and so are the angles under it (red).</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/05.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.5, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let ABC be an isosceles triangle having the side AB equal to the side AC;

and let the straight lines BD, CE be produced further in a straight line with AB, AC. [Post. 2]

I say that the angle ABC is equal to the angle ACB, and the angle CBD to the angle BCE.

Let a point F be taken at random on BD;

from AE the greater let AG be cut off equal to AF the less; [I. 3]

and let the straight lines FC, GB be joined. [Post. 1]

Then, since AF is equal to AG and AB to AC,

the two sides FA, AC are equal to the two sides GA, AB, respectively;

and they contain a common angle, the angle FAG.

Therefore the base FC is equal to the base GB,

and the triangle AFC is equal to the triangle AGB,

and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend,

that is, the angle ACF to the angle ABG,

and the angle AFC to the angle AGB. [I. 4]

And, since the whole AF is equal to the whole AG,

and in these AB is equal to AC,

the remainder BF is equal to the remainder CG.

But FC was also proved equal to GB;

therefore the two sides BF, FC are equal to the two sides CG, GB respectively;

and the angle BFC is equal to the angle CGB,

while the base BC is common to them;

therefore the triangle BFC is also equal to the triangle CGB,

and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend;

therefore the angle FBC is equal to the angle GCB,

and the angle BCF to the angle CBG.

Accordingly, since the whole angle ABG was proved equal to the angle ACF,

and in these the angle CBG is equal to the angle BCF,

the remaining angle ABC is equal to the remaining angle ACB;

and they are at the base of the triangle ABC.

But the angle FBC was also proved equal to the angle GCB;

and they are under the base.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

```lean
/-! ## What Euclid reads off the figure -/

/-- Order on a straight line: if `Y` is between `X` and `Z`, and `Z` is between `X` and
`W`, then `Z` is between `Y` and `W`. -/
theorem Prop5.between_inner {X Y Z W : Point} (h₁ : Between X Y Z) (h₂ : Between X Z W) :
    Between Y Z W := by
  obtain ⟨L, hX, hZ⟩ := Postulate1 X Z (ne_of_between_ends h₁)
  have hY : OnLine Y L := on_line_of_between_ends h₁ hX hZ
  have hW : OnLine W L := on_line_of_between h₂ hX hZ
  have hYZ : Y ≠ Z := (ne_of_between (between_symm h₁)).symm
  have hZW : Z ≠ W := (ne_of_between (between_symm h₂)).symm
  have hYW : Y ≠ W := by
    rintro rfl
    exact not_between_of_between (between_symm h₂) (between_symm h₁)
  /- Of the three points Y, Z, W one is between the other two; only Z can be. -/
  rcases between_cases hYZ hZW hYW hY hZ hW with h | h | h
  · exact h
  · exact absurd (between_of_between_left (between_symm h₂) (between_symm h))
      (not_between_of_between_between h (between_symm h₁))
  · exact absurd (between_of_between_left (between_symm h₁) (between_symm h))
      (not_between_of_between (between_symm h₂))

/-- Euclid's "chance point" `F` on `BD`. He takes it at random, but in the very next
breath calls `AE` "the greater" and `AF` "the less", so `F` must not lie too far out
along `BD`. A circle about `A`, larger than `AB` but smaller than `AE`, keeps it in:
`F` is taken on `BD` inside that circle, or where `BD` leaves it. -/
theorem Prop5.chance_point {A B C D E : Point} (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖A C‖) (hD : Between A B D)
    (hE : Between A C E) : ∃ F : Point, Between B F D ∧ ‖A F‖ < ‖A E‖ := by
  obtain ⟨AE, hA_AE, hE_AE⟩ := Postulate1 A E (ne_of_between_ends hE)
  have hC_AE : OnLine C AE := on_line_of_between_ends hE hA_AE hE_AE
  have hCE : C ≠ E := (ne_of_between (between_symm hE)).symm
  /- A point X between C and E: then AX is less than AE and greater than AC. -/
  obtain ⟨X, -, hCXE, -⟩ := exists_point_between hC_AE hE_AE hCE []
  have hAXE : Between A X E :=
    between_symm (between_of_between_left (between_symm hE) (between_symm hCXE))
  have hACX : Between A C X :=
    between_symm (Prop5.between_inner (between_symm hCXE) (between_symm hE))
  have hAX_AE : ‖A X‖ < ‖A E‖ := by
    rw [← len_add_of_between hAXE]
    exact CommonNotion5 (len_pos (ne_of_between (between_symm hAXE)).symm)
  have hAB_AX : ‖A B‖ < ‖A X‖ := by
    rw [hAB, ← len_add_of_between hACX]
    exact CommonNotion5 (len_pos (ne_of_between (between_symm hACX)).symm)
  obtain ⟨α, hA_α, hX_α⟩ := Postulate3 A X (ne_of_between hAXE)
  have hB_α : InsideCircle B α := inside_of_len_lt hA_α hX_α hAB_AX
  have hBD : B ≠ D := (ne_of_between (between_symm hD)).symm
  obtain ⟨BD, hB_BD, hD_BD⟩ := Postulate1 B D hBD
  by_cases hD_α : InsideCircle D α ∨ OnCircle D α
  · /- D is not outside the circle: any point between B and D is inside it. -/
    obtain ⟨F, -, hBFD, -⟩ := exists_point_between hB_BD hD_BD hBD []
    have hF_α : InsideCircle F α := inside_of_between (Or.inl hB_α) hD_α hBFD
    exact ⟨F, hBFD, lt_trans (len_lt_of_inside hA_α hX_α hF_α) hAX_AE⟩
  · /- D is outside: take F where BD crosses the circle (System E, Intersections 4). -/
    have hD_out : OutsideCircle D α := ⟨fun h => hD_α (Or.inl h), fun h => hD_α (Or.inr h)⟩
    obtain ⟨F, hF_α, -, hBFD⟩ := line_circle_between hB_α hB_BD hD_out hD_BD
    exact ⟨F, hBFD, by rw [Definition15 hA_α hF_α hX_α]; exact hAX_AE⟩

/-- `G` is cut off from `AE`, and `AG` is greater than `AC`; so `G` lies beyond `C`. -/
theorem Prop5.beyond {A C G E : Point} (hACE : Between A C E) (hAGE : Between A G E)
    (h : ‖A C‖ < ‖A G‖) : Between A C G := by
  obtain ⟨L, hA, hE⟩ := Postulate1 A E (ne_of_between_ends hACE)
  have hC : OnLine C L := on_line_of_between_ends hACE hA hE
  have hG : OnLine G L := on_line_of_between_ends hAGE hA hE
  have hCG : C ≠ G := by
    rintro rfl
    exact lt_irrefl _ h
  rcases between_cases (ne_of_between hACE) hCG (ne_of_between hAGE) hA hC hG with h' | h' | h'
  · exact h'
  · /- A between C and G: then A would be between C and E. -/
    exact absurd (between_of_between_right h' hAGE) (not_between_of_between hACE)
  · /- G between A and C: then AG would be only a part of AC. -/
    have hpart : ‖A G‖ < ‖A C‖ := by
      rw [← len_add_of_between h']
      exact CommonNotion5 (len_pos (ne_of_between (between_symm h')).symm)
    exact absurd (lt_trans h hpart) (lt_irrefl _)

/-- Two points of a straight line and a third point off it make a triangle. -/
theorem Prop5.triangle {P Q R : Point} {L : Line} (hP : OnLine P L) (hQ : OnLine Q L)
    (hPQ : P ≠ Q) (hR : ¬ OnLine R L) : Triangle P Q R := by
  rintro ⟨M, hPM, hQM, hRM⟩
  exact hR (line_unique hPQ hPM hQM hP hQ ▸ hRM)

/-- An angle is not changed when one of its arms is traced through another point of the
same ray: if `P` is between `V` and `P'`, the angle `P'VQ` is the angle `PVQ`.
(System E, diagram-angle transfer 4) -/
theorem Prop5.angle_along {V P P' Q : Point} (h : Between V P P') (hQV : Q ≠ V) :
    ∠ P' V Q = ∠ P V Q := by
  have hVP : V ≠ P := ne_of_between h
  obtain ⟨L, hV, hP⟩ := Postulate1 V P hVP
  obtain ⟨M, hVM, hQM⟩ := Postulate1 V Q hQV.symm
  have hP' : OnLine P' L := on_line_of_between h hV hP
  exact angle_eq_of_same_rays hV hP' hP hVM hQM hQM (ne_of_between_ends h).symm hVP.symm
    hQV hQV (fun h' => not_between_of_between h (between_symm h'))
    (fun h' => ne_of_between_ends h' rfl)

/-- If `R` lies between `P` and `Q`, and `V` is off the straight line `PQ`, then `VR`
falls within the angle `PVQ`, and that angle is made up of `PVR` and `RVQ`.
(System E, Pasch 2 and diagram-angle transfer 2) -/
theorem Prop5.angle_add {V P Q R : Point} {L M N : Line} (hVL : OnLine V L) (hPL : OnLine P L)
    (hVM : OnLine V M) (hQM : OnLine Q M) (hPN : OnLine P N) (hQN : OnLine Q N)
    (hVN : ¬ OnLine V N) (h : Between P R Q) : ∠ P V Q = ∠ P V R + ∠ R V Q := by
  have hRN : OnLine R N := on_line_of_between_ends h hPN hQN
  have hVP : V ≠ P := fun e => hVN (e ▸ hPN)
  have hVQ : V ≠ Q := fun e => hVN (e ▸ hQN)
  have hPQ : P ≠ Q := ne_of_between_ends h
  have hPR : P ≠ R := ne_of_between h
  have hRQ : R ≠ Q := (ne_of_between (between_symm h)).symm
  have hLM : L ≠ M := by
    rintro rfl
    exact hVN (line_unique hPQ hPL hQM hPN hQN ▸ hVL)
  have hRL : ¬ OnLine R L := fun hR => hVN (line_unique hPR hPL hR hPN hRN ▸ hVL)
  have hRM : ¬ OnLine R M := fun hR => hVN (line_unique hRQ hR hQM hRN hQN ▸ hVM)
  exact angle_add_of_inside hVL hVM hPL hQM hVP hVQ hRL hRM hLM
    (same_side_symm (pasch2 (between_symm h) hQM hRM))
    (same_side_symm (pasch2 h hPL hRL))

/-- In isosceles triangles the angles at the base are equal to one another, and, if the equal
straight lines be produced further, the angles under the base will be equal to one another. -/
theorem Prop5 {A B C D E : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖A C‖)
    (hD : Between A B D) (hE : Between A C E) :
    ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B ∧ ∠ C B D = ∠ B C E := by
  -- Let ABC be an isosceles triangle having the side AB equal to the side AC;
  have hA_B : A ≠ B := hABC.ne₁₂
  have hB_C : B ≠ C := hABC.ne₂₃
  have hA_C : A ≠ C := hABC.ne₁₃
  -- and let the straight lines BD, CE be produced further in a straight line with AB,
  -- AC. [Post. 2]
  /- The statement hands us D and E already produced, so Lean needs no Postulate 2.
     It does need the straight lines AB and AC themselves, with D and E on them, and
     the fact that ABC is a triangle: C is off AB, and B is off AC. -/
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hA_B
  obtain ⟨AC, hA_AC, hC_AC⟩ := Postulate1 A C hA_C
  have hC_AB : ¬ OnLine C AB := fun h => hABC ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB, h⟩
  have hB_AC : ¬ OnLine B AC := fun h => hABC ⟨AC, hA_AC, h, hC_AC⟩
  have hE_AC : OnLine E AC := on_line_of_between hE hA_AC hC_AC
  -- I say that the angle ABC is equal to the angle ACB, and the angle CBD to the angle BCE.
  -- Let a point F be taken at random on BD;
  /- At random, but not too far out: see `Prop5.chance_point`. Then F lies beyond B
     on the straight line AB. -/
  obtain ⟨F, hBFD, hAF_AE⟩ := Prop5.chance_point hAB hD hE
  have hABF : Between A B F :=
    between_symm (Prop5.between_inner (between_symm hBFD) (between_symm hD))
  have hF_AB : OnLine F AB := on_line_of_between hABF hA_AB hB_AB
  have hA_F : A ≠ F := ne_of_between_ends hABF
  -- from AE the greater let AG be cut off equal to AF the less; [I. 3]
  obtain ⟨G, hAGE, hAG_AF⟩ := Prop3 hA_F hAF_AE
  have hG_AC : OnLine G AC := on_line_of_between_ends hAGE hA_AC hE_AC
  have hA_G : A ≠ G := ne_of_between hAGE
  -- and let the straight lines FC, GB be joined. [Post. 1]
  have hF_C : F ≠ C := fun h => hC_AB (h ▸ hF_AB)
  have hG_B : G ≠ B := fun h => hB_AC (h ▸ hG_AC)
  obtain ⟨FC, hF_FC, hC_FC⟩ := Postulate1 F C hF_C
  obtain ⟨GB, hG_GB, hB_GB⟩ := Postulate1 G B hG_B
  -- Then, since AF is equal to AG and AB to AC,
  have hAF_AG : ‖A F‖ = ‖A G‖ := hAG_AF.symm
  -- the two sides FA, AC are equal to the two sides GA, AB, respectively;
  have hAC_AB : ‖A C‖ = ‖A B‖ := hAB.symm
  -- and they contain a common angle, the angle FAG.
  /- Common, because B lies on AF and C lies on AG. For C that takes a word Euclid
     doesn't say: AG, being equal to AF, is greater than AB, that is, than AC; so G
     lies beyond C. -/
  have hAB_AF : ‖A B‖ < ‖A F‖ := by
    rw [← len_add_of_between hABF]
    exact CommonNotion5 (len_pos (ne_of_between hBFD))
  have hACG : Between A C G :=
    Prop5.beyond hE hAGE (by rw [hAC_AB, ← hAF_AG]; exact hAB_AF)
  have hFAC_GAB : ∠ F A C = ∠ G A B := by
    rw [Prop5.angle_along hABF hA_C.symm, angle_symm hA_B.symm hA_C.symm,
      Prop5.angle_along hACG hA_B.symm]
  -- Therefore the base FC is equal to the base GB,
  have hAFC : Triangle A F C := Prop5.triangle hA_AB hF_AB hA_F hC_AB
  have hAGB : Triangle A G B := Prop5.triangle hA_AC hG_AC hA_G hB_AC
  have hI4 := Prop4 hAFC hAGB hAF_AG hAC_AB hFAC_GAB
  have hFC_GB : ‖F C‖ = ‖G B‖ := hI4.1
  -- and the triangle AFC is equal to the triangle AGB,
  have : △ A F C = △ A G B := hI4.2.1
  -- and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those
  -- which the equal sides subtend,
  -- that is, the angle ACF to the angle ABG,
  have hACF_ABG : ∠ A C F = ∠ A B G := hI4.2.2.2
  -- and the angle AFC to the angle AGB. [I. 4]
  have hAFC_AGB : ∠ A F C = ∠ A G B := hI4.2.2.1
  -- And, since the whole AF is equal to the whole AG,
  have hAB_BF : ‖A B‖ + ‖B F‖ = ‖A F‖ := len_add_of_between hABF
  have hAC_CG : ‖A C‖ + ‖C G‖ = ‖A G‖ := len_add_of_between hACG
  -- and in these AB is equal to AC,
  -- the remainder BF is equal to the remainder CG.
  have hBF_CG : ‖B F‖ = ‖C G‖ := by
    apply CommonNotion3 (c := ‖A B‖) (d := ‖A C‖) _ hAB
    rw [add_comm, hAB_BF, hAF_AG, ← hAC_CG, add_comm]
  -- But FC was also proved equal to GB;
  -- therefore the two sides BF, FC are equal to the two sides CG, GB respectively;
  have hFB_GC : ‖F B‖ = ‖G C‖ := by rw [len_symm F B, hBF_CG, len_symm C G]
  -- and the angle BFC is equal to the angle CGB,
  /- These are the angles AFC and AGB over again, since B lies on FA and C on GA. -/
  have hBFC_CGB : ∠ B F C = ∠ C G B := by
    rw [← Prop5.angle_along (between_symm hABF) hF_C.symm,
      ← Prop5.angle_along (between_symm hACG) hG_B.symm]
    exact hAFC_AGB
  -- while the base BC is common to them;
  /- Euclid is quoting I.4 ahead of time, as Heath explains: the bases are equal
     because they are one and the same base. -/
  -- therefore the triangle BFC is also equal to the triangle CGB,
  have hFBC : Triangle F B C :=
    Prop5.triangle hF_AB hB_AB (ne_of_between (between_symm hABF)) hC_AB
  have hGCB : Triangle G C B :=
    Prop5.triangle hG_AC hC_AC (ne_of_between (between_symm hACG)) hB_AC
  have hI4' := Prop4 hFBC hGCB hFB_GC hFC_GB hBFC_CGB
  have : △ B F C = △ C G B := by
    rw [← area_rotate F C B, ← area_swap F B C, hI4'.2.1, area_swap G C B, area_rotate G B C]
  -- and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those
  -- which the equal sides subtend;
  -- therefore the angle FBC is equal to the angle GCB,
  have hFBC_GCB : ∠ F B C = ∠ G C B := hI4'.2.2.1
  -- and the angle BCF to the angle CBG.
  have hBCF_CBG : ∠ B C F = ∠ C B G := by
    rw [angle_symm hB_C hF_C, angle_symm hB_C.symm hG_B]
    exact hI4'.2.2.2
  -- Accordingly, since the whole angle ABG was proved equal to the angle ACF,
  /- Whole, because C lies between A and G, so that BC falls within the angle ABG;
     likewise B lies between A and F, so that CB falls within the angle ACF. -/
  have hABG : ∠ A B G = ∠ A B C + ∠ C B G :=
    Prop5.angle_add hB_AB hA_AB hB_GB hG_GB hA_AC hG_AC hB_AC hACG
  have hACF : ∠ A C F = ∠ A C B + ∠ B C F :=
    Prop5.angle_add hC_AC hA_AC hC_FC hF_FC hA_AB hF_AB hC_AB hABF
  -- and in these the angle CBG is equal to the angle BCF,
  -- the remaining angle ABC is equal to the remaining angle ACB;
  have hbase : ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B := by
    apply CommonNotion3 (c := ∠ C B G) (d := ∠ B C F) _ hBCF_CBG.symm
    rw [← hABG, ← hACF, hACF_ABG]
  -- and they are at the base of the triangle ABC.
  -- But the angle FBC was also proved equal to the angle GCB;
  -- and they are under the base.
  /- Under the base: the angle CBD is the angle CBF, since F lies on BD, and the angle
     BCE is the angle BCG, since G lies between C and E. -/
  have hCGE : Between C G E := Prop5.between_inner hACG hAGE
  have hunder : ∠ C B D = ∠ B C E := by
    rw [angle_symm hB_C.symm (ne_of_between (between_symm hD)),
      Prop5.angle_along hBFD hB_C.symm, hFBC_GCB, ← Prop5.angle_along hCGE hB_C,
      angle_symm (ne_of_between (between_symm hE)) hB_C]
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hbase, hunder⟩
  -- Q. E. D.
```

<details><summary>The 44 things Euclid takes for granted here</summary>

**Reading the figure**

- [`between_cases`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L70): Of three different points on a straight line, one is between the other two. (Between 6)
- [`between_of_between_left`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L63): (Between 4)
- [`between_of_between_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L66): (Between 5)
- [`between_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L41): If `B` is between `A` and `C`, it is between `C` and `A`. (Between 1)
- [`centre_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L33): The centre of a circle is inside it. (Generalities 3)
- [`circles_meet`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L178): If each circle passes through a point inside the other, the circles cut one another. This is the step Euclid takes for granted in I.1. (Intersection 5)
- [`exists_point`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L26): Let a point be taken. (Points 1)
- [`exists_point_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L38): Let a point be taken between `B` and `C`. (Points 3)
- [`inside_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L140): A circle is "convex": between two points on or inside it, every point is inside. (Circle 2)
- [`line_circle_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L69): A straight line through a point `B` inside a circle, heading out to a point `C` outside it, cuts the circle between `B` and `C`. (Intersections 4)
- [`line_circle_beyond`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L75): A straight line through a point `B` inside a circle, produced beyond `B` away from `C`, cuts the circle there. (Intersections 5)
- [`line_unique`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L26): Two points determine a straight line. (Generalities 1)
- [`ne_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L44): A point between two others differs from the first. (Between 1)
- [`ne_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L47): The ends of a finite straight line differ. (Between 1)
- [`not_between_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L50): If `B` is between `A` and `C`, then `A` is not between `B` and `C`. (Between 1)
- [`not_between_of_between_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L74): (Between 7)
- [`not_on_line_of_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L86): Points on one side of a line are not on it. (Same side 3)
- [`on_line_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L54): A straight line through `A` and `B`, with `B` between `A` and `C`, passes through `C`. (Between 2)
- [`on_line_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L59): A straight line through `A` and `C` passes through every point between them. (Between 3)
- [`pasch2`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L101): (Pasch 2)
- [`pasch3`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L104): A line through a point between `A` and `C` separates them. (Pasch 3)
- [`same_side_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L83): (Same side 2)
- [`triple_incidence2`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L121): (Triple incidence 2)

**Lengths, angles and areas**

- [`angle_add_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L54): If `D` lies within the angle `BAC`, then `BAC` is made up of `BAD` and `DAC`. (Diagram-angle 2)
- [`angle_eq_of_same_rays`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L72): The angle doesn't change if its arms are traced through other points on the same rays. (Diagram-angle 4)
- [`angle_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L26): The angle `ABC` is the angle `CBA`. (Metric 4)
- [`area_congruent`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L43): Triangles equal in all their sides and angles are equal in area. Euclid uses this without comment once he has shown two triangles congruent. (Metric 9)
- [`area_rotate`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L35): The triangle `ABC` is the triangle `CAB`. (Metric 8)
- [`area_swap`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L38): The triangle `ABC` is the triangle `ACB`. (Metric 8)
- [`eq_of_len_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L17): A finite straight line with distinct ends has length. (Metric 1)
- [`inside_of_len_lt`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L33): A point nearer the centre than the circumference is inside. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_add_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L21): If `B` is between `A` and `C`, then `AB` and `BC` together make up `AC`. (Diagram-segment 1)
- [`len_lt_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L37): A point inside is nearer the centre than the circumference. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_self`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L20): The "line" from a point to itself has no length. (Metric 1)
- [`len_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L23): The line `AB` is the line `BA`. (Metric 3)
- [`same_ray_of_angle_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L49): If the angle `BAC` is nothing, `C` lies on the ray from `A` through `B`. (Diagram-angle 1)

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L29): **Superposition.** The triangle `ABC` can be applied to the straight line `L` with `A` on `D`, `B` on the ray from `D` through `G`, and `C` on the side of `L` where `H` is, without changing any side or angle.

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L25): Adding is commutative. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L44): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L28): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L31): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L34): "Less than" is transitive. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L38): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L41): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

</details>

## Mishnah

**Thales, and a proof of Euclid's own.** Proclus credits the discovery to Thales, "who however is said to have spoken of the angles as being *similar*, and not as being equal" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 252). The proof, though, seems to be new. A passage of Aristotle shows the older textbooks reaching this theorem through the "mixed" angles of circles, and Heath concludes: "It is a natural inference from the passage of Aristotle that Euclid's proof of I. 5 was his own" (vol. 1, pp. 253–254). Generations of schoolchildren knew it as the *pons asinorum*, the bridge of asses.

**A chance point, but not too far out.** Euclid takes F "at random" on BD; the Greek, Heath notes, means "a chance point" (vol. 1, p. 252). In the very next sentence he calls AE "the greater" and AF "the less", so F must not lie too far along BD. For Euclid that costs nothing, since the sides are produced as far as we please. Here D and E are given, so `Prop5.chance_point` keeps F inside a circle about A drawn a little smaller than AE: anywhere between B and D if D is inside that circle, or where BD leaves it if not (System E, Circle 2 and Intersections 4). That circle is why Postulate 3 and Definition 15 are on the certificate, though Euclid cites neither. Postulate 2 is not, because the statement hands us D and E already produced.

**What Lean made us say.** Euclid's figure quietly settles the order of its points, and Lean wants each of those facts said. G lies beyond C, because AG, being equal to AF, is greater than AC (`Prop5.beyond`). The angle FAG is "common" to the two triangles because B lies on AF and C on AG, and an angle doesn't change when an arm is traced through another point of the same ray (`Prop5.angle_along`, System E's diagram-angle transfer 4). The "whole angle ABG" really is made up of ABC and CBG, because C lies between A and G and so BC falls within it (`Prop5.angle_add`, from Pasch 2 and diagram-angle transfer 2). And one fact of order on a line, `Prop5.between_inner`, says that if B is between A and D and F between B and D, then B is between A and F. Every rule cited is one of Avigad, Dean and Mumma's, read with LeanEuclid's Lean version open alongside; Beeson, Narboux and Wiedijk's *Proof-checking Euclid* is a fine guide to how many such facts of order hide in Euclid's figures. With them in hand, the proof is Euclid's own: I.3 to cut off AG, I.4 twice, then Common Notion 3 twice.

**The base that is common.** "While the base BC is common to them" looks idle, and Todhunter, Heath tells us, "left out these words as being of no use and tending to perplex a beginner. But Euclid evidently chose to quote the conclusion of I. 4 exactly" (vol. 1, p. 252). Lean agrees with Euclid: the second use of I.4 hands back the equation ‖BC‖ = ‖CB‖, two bases that are equal because they are the same base.

**Pappus' shortcut.** Proclus reports a proof by Pappus with no construction at all: "Let us conceive this one triangle as two triangles," ABC and ACB, and apply I.4. Heath: "It seems to me that the form given to the proof by Pappus himself is by far the best" (vol. 1, p. 254). He has less patience for the classroom version in which the triangle is lifted and turned over: "There is the obvious difficulty that it supposes the triangle to be taken up and at the same time to remain where it is" (vol. 1, p. 254). In Lean, Pappus' proof is a single citation of I.4, with ABC as both triangles: `(Prop4 hABC hACB hAB hAB.symm (angle_symm …)).2.2.1`. It is also how Hilbert, who made side–angle–side an axiom, gets the base angles. But it "does not include the proof of the second part of the proposition about the angles under the base" (vol. 1, p. 255), and this book follows Euclid's own road.

**Why the angles under the base?** Heath admits the second part "is not necessary for any subsequent demonstration that is to be found in the original text of Euclid, but only for the interpolated second case of I. 7." He accepts Proclus' explanation, that it "was inserted for the purpose of fore-arming the learner against a possible objection" to I.7 as Euclid gives it, with one case only (vol. 1, p. 255).

**The modern way.** Put A at the origin and B, C at vectors b, c with |b| = |c|. Then cos B = b·(b − c)/(|b||b − c|) and cos C = c·(c − b)/(|c||c − b|), and both numerators equal |b|² − b·c. Or, in Pappus' spirit: the reflection in the line along b + c swaps b and c, and so carries each base angle onto the other.
